passages.title: Are festivals becoming too commercial?
passages.text:
[A] In the weeks before major festivals, shops in many cities fill with decorations, special offers and seasonal products. For businesses, festivals have become some of the most important times of the year, and in some sectors, such as toys and confectionery, they account for a large share of annual sales. Critics argue that this commercialisation has turned meaningful traditions into shopping events.

[B] Surveys suggest that many people share this concern. In one study carried out in five countries, more than half of the people questioned said that festivals had become “too much about spending money”. Interestingly, the same survey found that most of these people also said they enjoyed buying presents and special food. Researchers concluded that people’s feelings about commercialisation are often mixed rather than simply negative.

[C] Supporters of festival trade point out that buying and selling have always been part of celebrations. Historical records show that many traditional festivals included markets where farmers sold produce and craftspeople sold their goods. Without this economic activity, they argue, many festivals would not have survived, and today local businesses still provide much of the funding for public events such as parades and concerts.

[D] Nevertheless, some communities have taken steps to protect the non-commercial side of their festivals. In certain towns, advertising is banned in the main square during the festival period, and some organisers have introduced free events, such as storytelling and traditional games, which require no spending at all. Religious and community groups also continue to hold ceremonies that have little connection with shopping.

[E] For individuals, the solution may be a matter of choice. Many families now set a spending limit or agree to exchange handmade gifts, and some spend part of the festival volunteering, for example by preparing meals for people who live alone. Such practices suggest that it is possible to enjoy the commercial side of festivals without allowing it to replace their deeper meaning. As one festival organiser put it, the best celebrations are remembered for the people who were there, not for what was bought.

coach.message: Bài “Second reading: commercialisation of festivals”: Phân biệt nguyên nhân, lợi ích và rủi ro của thương mại hóa lễ hội. Trước khi thử, hãy nói một việc bạn sẽ kiểm tra ở bài này.

Bạn đang xem “premium seating” (noun phrase), nghĩa là “chỗ ngồi hạng cao”. Ví dụ: “Premium seating costs more than general entry.”. Hãy tạo một câu mới liên quan đến second reading: commercialisation of festivals thay vì chép lại.
Ở ví dụ có hướng dẫn “What was one benefit of ticket sales?”, hãy làm bước này trước: Look for a trade-off and identify who benefits and who loses. Chỉ mở mẫu sau khi tự thử.

Lỗi dễ gặp ở bài “Second reading: commercialisation of festivals”: Không khẳng định tất cả cư dân đều phản đối. Paid performers là lợi ích được nêu trực tiếp, song song với phàn nàn mất chỗ ngồi miễn phí.

Bạn đã hoàn thành bài “Second reading: commercialisation of festivals”. Hãy đánh dấu bằng chứng trong văn bản; lưu cụm “premium seating” nếu thực sự muốn dùng lại, rồi sửa một chỗ chưa chắc chắn trước khi làm bài mới.
Bài này mình luyện TFNG với số liệu và ý kiến về thương mại hóa. Hãy đọc đoạn rồi tìm phần nào trả lời đúng câu hỏi; chưa cần đoán ngay.
Bạn đang bị bẫy: NOT GIVEN: bài nói rõ phạm vi khảo sát. Hãy đọc bằng chứng “exactly five countries” rồi thử lại.
Hãy phân biệt: FALSE: bài không khẳng định chiều ngược. Bằng chứng cần đối chiếu là “did not compare how much families in different age groups spent”.
Bạn đã tìm đúng cả hai bằng chứng. Hãy vào phần luyện độc lập; Coach sẽ không tự chen vào.
